---
title: "Day 2 · Regression and an introduction to data science"
---

Two hours of theory followed by two hours of guided practical work in R, ending with the final exercise.

## Learning objectives

By the end of Day 2 you will be able to:

- Explain the difference between describing, estimating associations, predicting and discovering groups
- Use a scatterplot and correlation to describe a relationship, and explain why association is not causation
- Fit and interpret simple and multiple linear regression models in R
- Explain confounding and mediation, and interpret an adjusted association
- Check a linear regression model using residual plots, and plot fitted relationships
- Read the output of a logistic and a Poisson regression (OR, aOR, IRR) at an introductory level
- Describe what k-means clustering does, why scaling matters, and why clusters need checking

Linear regression is practised in full. Logistic regression, Poisson regression and clustering are introductions with guided code: the aim is to read and question the output, not to master the methods in one afternoon.

## Confounding at a glance

![Activity coefficient for systolic blood pressure, crude, adjusted for age and sex (confounders) and also adjusted for BMI (a mediator). Simulated teaching data.](../../downloads/figures/f_crude_adjusted.png){fig-alt="Point estimates with 95% confidence intervals for the activity coefficient in three regression models."}

::: {.key-findings}
**Key messages of Day 2.** Choose adjustment variables from a causal diagram, not from p-values. Adjust for confounders; do not adjust for mediators when you want the total effect. An odds ratio is not a risk ratio when the outcome is common. Clusters are a description to be checked, not a discovery to be believed.
:::
